title.text: Foundation models: pretraining, post-training, model families, reasoning and multimodal models, benchmarks

objects.text: What is a foundation model, how does it become an assistant, and what does a benchmark score tell me?

Applied AI and Automation  |  Session 6 of 14
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome to Session 6. Last time you saw how a language model picks its next word. Today we ask how a model like that becomes the assistant you use, what the main kinds of model are, and how to judge claims about them. You see one task answered by two assistants, recorded, and you read a real model card.

The question for today is this: What is a foundation model, how does it become an assistant, and what does a benchmark score tell me? Keep it in mind. At the end of the session we come back to it and see how much more you can say.

title.text:
Your two hours: most of
the time is your own work

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_plan_11.90x3.95_49455d2e.png
objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: You see one task answered by two assistants, then read a real model card yourself.

slides.notes:
The first half hour gives you the big picture of how a foundation model is made: pretraining like reading a library, then post-training like coaching. We cover the main kinds of model and what a benchmark can and cannot tell you. Then I show one task answered by two different assistants, recorded.

After the break you read a real model card on paper and build a comparison grid for your own tasks.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  What is a token?
2.  What does temperature do?
3.  Why can a fluent answer be wrong?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_question_2.80.png

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 5. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. What is a token? Take a moment.

A good answer is this. A piece of text a model reads and writes: a short word, part of a long word, a number or a mark.

Question two. What does temperature do? Say it to yourself first.

A good answer is this. It sharpens or flattens the percentages before a piece is picked. Low repeats the favourite, high gives variety and then nonsense.

Question three. Why can a fluent answer be wrong? Think about your own task as you answer.

A good answer is this. The model always produces a likely next piece. Nothing in that loop checks the facts, unless search or files are added.

If an answer was missing, your own task card or last workbook page has it. Now to today.

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: A large model trained on a vast amount of text, images or both, that many products are built on.
The first stage: reading huge amounts of data to learn to guess the next piece.
The coaching stage that turns a base model into an assistant that follows instructions.
A fixed set of questions with a score, used to compare models.
The page a maker publishes about a model: licence, size, uses and limits.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Foundation model. A large model trained on a vast amount of text, images or both, that many products are built on.

Pretraining. The first stage: reading huge amounts of data to learn to guess the next piece.

Post-training. The coaching stage that turns a base model into an assistant that follows instructions.

Benchmark. A fixed set of questions with a score, used to compare models.

Model card. The page a maker publishes about a model: licence, size, uses and limits.

title.text:
Pretraining is reading a
library to guess the next word

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t06_library_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Pretraining is reading a library to guess the next word

objects.text: A foundation model starts by reading an enormous library of text.

runs.text: Hide the next word, guess it, adjust.
GPT-2 read about 40 GB of web pages.

slides.notes:
Think of a student locked in a huge library with one job: read a passage, cover the next word, guess it, then check and adjust. Repeat billions of times. That is pretraining. It needs vast amounts of data and computing power, which is why only a few organisations do it from scratch.

The result is called a base model or foundation model, because many products are built on it. GPT-2, the model from Session 5, read about forty gigabytes of web pages, according to its model card. A base model only continues text. It does not yet follow your instructions.

title.text:
Post-training is coaching: a base
model becomes an assistant

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t06_coach_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Post-training is coaching: a base model becomes an assistant

objects.text: Coaching teaches the model to follow instructions and give answers people prefer.

runs.text: People write good answers, then rank answers.
In a 2022 study, a coached 1.3 billion model was preferred over an uncoached 175 billion one.

slides.notes:
Reading a library does not teach manners. Post-training is the coaching. In the first step people write good answers to many instructions and the model learns from them. In the second step people rank several answers, and the model learns to produce the kind people prefer. A 2022 paper from OpenAI, called InstructGPT, found that people preferred answers from a coached model with one point three billion adjustable numbers over the uncoached model with one hundred and seventy-five billion.

Coaching can matter as much as size. Today I show you the difference with real runs.

title.text:
The same task text: a base model
rambles and a coached model answers

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t06_base_vs_instruct_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: The same task text: a base model rambles and a coached model answers

objects.text: Real runs, 6 November 2026, on this laptop. Greedy decoding, so the outputs repeat.

slides.notes:
Here is the difference, recorded. I gave both models the same task text, about a damaged delivery at Nile Valley Foods. On the left, GPT-2 is a base model. It has never been coached. It behaves as if the text were the start of a news page and writes the company has not responded to requests for comment, over and over.

On the right, Qwen two point five, one point five billion, is a small coached open model. It follows the three instructions: a label, a sum and a reply. Same machine type, different coaching. That is the gap between a base model and an assistant.

title.text:
Three families to know: hosted assistants,
open weights and small local models

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t06_families_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Three families to know: hosted assistants, open weights and small local models

objects.text: Open weights means the learned numbers can be downloaded. Session 7 goes deeper.

slides.notes:
Here are the families you will meet. A hosted assistant runs on the maker computers. You send text and get text back, so you check the terms and the data settings. Examples are Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini. I say nothing about their insides, because their makers have not published them.

An open-weights model is one whose files of learned numbers you can download and run. GPT-2 is under the MIT licence. Qwen two point five and Mixtral are under Apache two point zero. A small local model is an open-weights model small enough for a laptop. Session 7 covers open weights in detail.

title.text:
Mixture of experts: a router sends
each piece to two of eight small blocks

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t06_moe_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Mixture of experts: a router sends each piece to two of eight small blocks

objects.text: Only a few experts work on each piece, so each piece needs less computing.

runs.text: Mixtral, 2024: 8 blocks per layer, 2 chosen per piece.
About 47 billion numbers in all, about 13 billion in use at a time.

slides.notes:
Some large models use a design called mixture of experts. Picture a hospital reception. Each patient is sent to just two of eight specialist teams. Inside the model, a small router looks at each piece and picks two of eight blocks of numbers, called experts, to work on it.

The Mixtral paper from January 2024 describes eight blocks per layer with two chosen for each piece. It reports about forty-seven billion numbers in total, with about thirteen billion in use for each piece. The benefit is less computing for each piece. The whole model still has to be stored, so it needs a lot of memory.

title.text:
Reasoning models write a long
working-out before the answer

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t06_reasoning_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Reasoning models write a long working-out before the answer

objects.text: They spend extra pieces thinking in steps, which can help on multi-step problems.

runs.text: The DeepSeek-R1 paper (2025) rewarded correct answers on checkable tasks.
Slower and dearer per answer.

slides.notes:
A reasoning model writes a long stretch of working before it gives the answer, like an accountant showing the steps of a reconciliation. Because it writes many more pieces, it takes longer and costs more, but it can do better on problems that need several steps. The DeepSeek-R1 paper, published in Nature in 2025, describes encouraging this by rewarding correct answers on tasks that can be checked, such as maths and coding.

I only describe the idea. I do not describe how any closed product works. Session 8 shows when to choose a reasoning model.

title.text:
Multimodal models turn images
and sound into pieces too

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t06_multimodal_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Multimodal models turn images and sound into pieces too

objects.text: Many current models accept more than text. Everything becomes pieces of numbers.

runs.text: A photo is cut into patches.
Useful for delivery notes, receipts and screenshots.

slides.notes:
A multimodal model accepts more than text. The trick is the same as before: turn everything into pieces of numbers. A photo is cut into small patches, a sound is cut into short slices, and each patch or slice becomes a piece the model can attend to, next to the text pieces.

This is why many assistants can read a photo of a delivery note or a receipt. It still makes mistakes, and it can misread a blurry figure. For your own work, test it on twenty real photos before you trust it on the twenty-first.

title.text: Image generators remove noise step by step

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t06_diffusion_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Image generators remove noise step by step

objects.text: The noise pictures are computed here. Diffusion models (DDPM, 2020) learn the reverse path.

slides.notes:
Image generators of the diffusion kind work with noise. In training, a clean picture is damaged step by step until only noise remains. That direction is easy, and I computed this row myself from a simple picture of a sack. The model learns the reverse path: given a noisy picture, remove a little noise.

To make an image, start from pure noise and apply that learned step many times. The foundational paper is Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models from 2020. One sentence is enough for most executives: image models turn noise into a picture, step by step.

title.text:
A benchmark is a fixed set
of questions with a score

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t06_bench_cards_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: A benchmark is a fixed set of questions with a score

objects.text: Facts from the original papers. Chatbot Arena ranks by human votes.

slides.notes:
You will see benchmark scores in every vendor pitch. A benchmark is a fixed set of questions with a score. MMLU, from 2020, covers fifty-seven subjects from elementary mathematics to law. GSM8K, from 2021, has about eight and a half thousand school maths word problems. HumanEval, from 2021, asks a model to write a program from a description and checks it by running it.

Chatbot Arena, from 2024, is different. People vote between two anonymous answers, and the ranking comes from the votes. Each one measures something narrow and real.

title.text:
A benchmark describes the benchmark;
your work is a different circle

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t06_bench_limits_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: A benchmark describes the benchmark; your work is a different circle

objects.text: A high score is a reason to test, and no reason to buy.

runs.text: Ask for the setup: prompt, tries, date.
Some questions may appear in the training text; outsiders cannot check.
Votes can reward style.

slides.notes:
What does a benchmark not tell you?

Whether the model suits your invoices, your clients and your rules. The two circles overlap only a little. Ask how the score was set up, because the prompt and the number of tries can change it. Some benchmark questions may appear in the training text, and outsiders cannot fully check that.

Human votes can reward a pleasant style over accuracy. A high score is a good reason to run your own test, and a poor reason to sign a contract. Your own ten-case sample, scored by you, is stronger evidence.

title.text: Demonstration: one task, two assistants, recorded

objects.text: I will show

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_flow_7.30x3.90_7a8b0a91.png
objects.alt: Demonstration: one task, two assistants, recorded

objects.text: Watch for

runs.text: The task asks for a label, a sum and a short reply.
Both get the same text and nothing else.
Look for invented promises.
The small model is not ChatGPT or Gemini.

slides.notes:
Now the recorded comparison. The task is the one on screen: a shop owner reports three wet and torn bags, mentions a payment, and asks what we will do. Both assistants got exactly the same text. Claude answered in a fresh session, with no hints. The other is Qwen two point five, one point five billion, a small open model that I ran on this laptop, three times.

Be fair to it: it is a small model, and it is not ChatGPT, Gemini or Claude. We score each reply on a checklist, and you watch especially for promises the company never made.

title.text:
Claude kept to the facts; the
small model invented a policy

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t06_two_answers_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Claude kept to the facts; the small model invented a policy

objects.text: Recorded 6 November 2026. Claude in a fresh subagent session. Not ChatGPT or Gemini.

slides.notes:
Here are the two replies. Claude wrote fifty-nine words, apologised, checked the payment against the price list, said the complaint was passed on and asked for photos. It promised no refund or date, because the task gave it none. The small model got the sum right, but then invented a policy.

In this run it said the shop owner must pay for only seventeen bags, and asked for a further payment, although payment was already made. The other two runs invented a waived shipping fee and a replacement. This is the next-word loop from Session 5 at work. Be fair: this is a hosted assistant of unpublished size against a model of one and a half billion numbers, so it says little about open against closed. Claude ran once, the small model three times.

title.text:
Scored on five checks: the small model
failed four of five in all three runs

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t06_scorecard_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Scored on five checks: the small model failed four of five in all three runs

objects.text: My own scoring of one task. It shows a pattern, and ranks no product.

slides.notes:
Here is the scorecard, and I must say it is my own judgement of one task. Claude passed all five checks. The small model computed the sum correctly in every run. It labelled the message billing. Billing is defensible, since the message mentions a payment, so treat that row as my judgement and the other four as clearer.

It wrote replies of about ninety to one hundred and twenty words against a limit of seventy. In every run it invented something the company never said, and it never flagged what it could not confirm. One task and three runs prove nothing about products in general. They show why you test a model on your own cases before you trust it.

title.text:
Reading two real model cards:
what is there and what is missing

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t06_model_card_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Reading two real model cards: what is there and what is missing

objects.text: From the published cards on Hugging Face, checked 6 November 2026.

slides.notes:
A model card is the page a maker publishes. Here are two real ones. Qwen two point five, one point five billion lists its licence, Apache two point zero, and its size, one point five four billion numbers. It lists a context of thirty-two thousand pieces and over twenty-nine languages, and says training had pretraining and post-training stages.

Its sections are introduction, requirements, quickstart, evaluation and citation, and I found no section on limitations. GPT-2 has a limitations and bias part. It says the model cannot tell fact from fiction and reflects its training data. What a card leaves out tells you as much as what it says.

title.text: Read a model card and ask four questions of it

objects.text: 15 minutes
Hands-on, no computer
Take the printed card for GPT-2. Answer four questions with a line from the card.

runs.text: What is the licence, and may you use it at work?
How big is it, and what was it trained on?
What does the maker say it should not be used for?
What is missing that you would want to know?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_sheet_5.50x3.55_010efdf2.png
objects.alt: What your finished page looks like

objects.text: You keep: The question sheet with a card line beside each answer.

slides.notes:
Now you read a model card yourself, on paper. I give you the printed GPT-2 card. Answer four questions, and write the line from the card beside each answer. What is the licence, and may you use it at work?

How big is the model, and what was it trained on?

What does the maker say it should not be used for?

And what is missing that you would want to know?

I have started the example sheet so you see the style. You have fifteen minutes. Then tell me one thing you would want to ask a vendor that no card answered.

grid for your own task

Hands-on, no computer
Fill one grid row for a real task of yours, with two models to try.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_sheet_5.50x3.55_fc7c38e2.png

This is your take-away. Write one task from your own work in a single line. Name two or three models you can reach, for example the assistant you already use and, if you like, an open model. Write ten real cases and the answer you expect for each.

Choose three checks that matter for that task, such as figures correct, label correct and nothing invented. The example shows two rows from Nile Valley Foods. Ten cases is enough to see a pattern. You may run the test in your own time. That part is optional.

slides.notes:
Here is the session turned into a table across the company. Reconciling invoices suits a reasoning model, and you check every total. Drafting replies suits a standard assistant, and you check for promises the company never made. Summarising CVs needs a private setting, and you check personal data and invented details.

Reading delivery note photos suits a multimodal model, tested on real photos, blurry ones too. Sensitive documents may suit an open model run in-house, and you check its licence and size. Poster images suit an image model, with brand and rights checks. These are starting points, never verdicts.

Pick the route you will take for your own task this month. A hosted assistant means you try the one you already have, on ten real cases. A reasoning model suits tasks where steps and figures matter. Open weights suits tasks where data must stay in-house, and I suggest you come back to that after Session 7.

Wait for evidence means you ask the vendor to run a test on your own sample. Tell me your task, your choice and the three checks from your grid. There is no best answer, only a reasoned one.
